task_brief: Day 4 of "Capstone Review, Defense, and Transition" (unit 6, grade 12) is an independent application on maintenance security and sunset planning. It is one step inside the unit — not the whole unit project — and takes about 60–90 minutes. The unit is working toward: Defend the capstone in a chosen private or public mode with complete documentation, a response to independent review, and a maintenance and transition plan. Today's work contributes to that by handling maintenance security and sunset planning at the independent application a stage, against the unit's wider topics of evidence assembly and documentation, independent review and critique response, limitations and future work, and maintenance security and sunset planning. This session produces reviewable evidence toward the unit performance task.
primary_task: Work independently on maintenance security and sunset planning in a situation nobody has worked for you. Define the inputs and the expected result before you build anything. Then produce the working artifact — code, an algorithm, a configuration, a labelled design, or a documented procedure — and demonstrate it on at least two inputs you chose, one ordinary and one edge case. Record the actual result beside the expected result for each. Where they differ, fix the artifact and note what the difference revealed about maintenance security and sunset planning. The activity_setup block below supplies the complete central input, exact specification, execution method, test cases, debugging target, and equal-credit manual simulation; use those exact materials rather than waiting for another handout, account, service, or tool. Anchor today's work inside its unit: this session's evidence is about maintenance security and sunset planning, and it belongs to "Capstone Review, Defense, and Transition", which also covers separate topics such as evidence assembly and documentation. Close out with this check before you stop: State your result for maintenance security and sunset planning and the single strongest piece of evidence supporting it. At grade 12 the bar is portfolio-quality independent work you could defend to an outside reader: intent stated, method justified, limitations named honestly, and revision traceable.

central_input.title: Inline fictional decision case for maintenance security and sunset planning
central_input.purpose: Classify and revise this case without opening a site, contacting anyone, signing in, or using real personal information.
scenario: A fictional app called Pebble Planner asks for a display nickname, exact birth date, home address, and contact list before showing a simple homework timer.
Its notice says the nickname is needed to label the timer, but gives no reason for collecting an address or contacts.
A fictional message then pressures the learner to reveal a sign-in secret immediately or lose the timer.
decision_options: B: stop, share no information, save a description of the message, and ask a trusted adult
C: invent an address but reveal a sign-in secret

presentation_and_privacy.sandbox_and_credentials_note: Everything in this task runs in a sandbox or on paper. Never use a real password, passphrase, API key, account credential, access token, precise home location, or any real person's identifiable information — invent fictional values instead. Do not sign into, probe, scan, stress, or attempt access to any live, production, school, or third-party system, and do not bypass a filter, licence, access control, or terms of service. Any practice login used in an example must be obviously invented — a silly made-up name paired with a nonsense multi-word phrase — and must never be anything you or anyone in your family actually uses somewhere real. If a task seems to need something real, substitute a made-up stand-in and note the substitution.

copyright_and_authorship: The graded submission must be your own authorship. A parent, tutor, or AI tool may explain an idea, demonstrate a technique, or give feedback on a draft, but must not produce, write, debug, or make any part of the work that is scored. Any code, asset, or text you did not write must be openly licensed or supplied for this task, and must be cited in a comment or note naming where it came from and what you changed.

For any multi-session project, supply a written milestone plan, checkpoint dates, and a task breakdown, so executive-function load is not silently part of what is being assessed.

task_accessibility_provisions: Provide a screen-reader-compatible editor, adjustable font size and contrast, and a complete keyboard-only workflow. An offline paper-and-trace route is available for every task here and is scored identically to an on-screen one.

This work spans sessions, so supply a written milestone plan, explicit checkpoint dates, and a task breakdown. Executive-function load — sequencing, holding the plan in mind, remembering where the work stopped — must not become a silent part of what is being assessed.
Breaks, extended time, a hidden timer, reduced copying, and a low-distraction setting are available on request and never reduce the score.
safety_and_privacy_rules: Allow a pause, break, or alternate response mode without treating it as failure.
Never use or require a real password, API key, access token, account credential, private message, precise location, or identifiable image; use clearly fictional placeholder values only.
Keep all security work in sandboxed, simulated, or fictional environments; never scan, probe, exploit, or attempt access against real systems, networks, accounts, services, or people.
Use approved sites and tools; do not bypass filters, access controls, licensing, or terms of service.
Treat AI output as a draft to verify and disclose. The tutor may explain concepts, ask diagnostic questions, and help debug, but never silently completes graded project work.

remediation: Reteaching for maintenance security and sunset planning follows the signal actually observed, not a fixed script. If the signal is "prerequisite gap": Return to the smallest prerequisite needed for maintenance security and sunset planning, model it in a concrete or text-only representation, then retry one fresh item. If the signal is "procedure without understanding": Ask the learner to explain or represent why the approach to maintenance security and sunset planning works before continuing. If the signal is "correct but low confidence": Confirm the reasoning specifically, offer one varied example of maintenance security and sunset planning, and avoid unnecessary remediation. If the signal is "repeated error pattern": Name the observable pattern neutrally, contrast it with a worked example, and schedule a short same-day or next-session review. If the signal is "requests the answer to graded work": Explain the concept, ask a diagnostic question, or help isolate the defect. Do not supply the graded artifact, solution code, or finished creative work. If the signal is "mastery evidence": Require accurate independent application plus explanation on a later or different occasion before marking maintenance security and sunset planning mastered. Re-check with one fresh item of the same kind before moving on, and record which signal was seen so the pattern is visible across the unit rather than treated as a one-off.
extension: Apply maintenance security and sunset planning under a new constraint, compare two approaches or perspectives, or explain the idea to someone else using an original example. Treat this as optional depth on maintenance security and sunset planning rather than extra volume: one harder case done well beats three more of the same. Extension work stays inside the same sandbox rules — no real credentials and no live external systems. Extension work is never required to reach mastery and must not be assigned as a penalty.
